rules.text: Freeze the five evaluation-defining choices before iterating; iterate only downstream of them.
Log every trial. Unlogged search is uncountable, and uncountable search cannot be adjusted for.
Run the tradability check *early*, not after signal refinement.
Prefer graceful degradation over optimal point estimates.
Regimes gate risk posture, never entry timing.
Drift is a flag; always follow it with a four-way diagnosis (data / feature / execution / regime).
Monitoring must distinguish signal decay from operational failure, or intervention becomes another overfitting channel.
AIC and similar in-sample criteria are unreliable for selecting interpretable structure — check separation diagnostics too.
Model-agnostic: this whole loop applies to rule-based systems as well.
Lock timestamp semantics, adjustment methodology, identifier policy, and revision handling *as pipeline metadata* before modeling.
Data errors are systematic, not random — design validation around the four alpha-manufacturing defects, in priority order: PIT → survivorship → corporate actions → identifiers.
Every cross-source join carries two time constraints (`available_at`, and `effective_date` ranges on ID mappings). Silent lookahead enters through joins that succeed.
PIT has three independent levels — values, universe, identifiers. Passing one proves nothing about the others.
Zero-lag records on delayed data are a red flag, always.
Represent instrument families at the right abstraction: options → surfaces, futures → raw contracts *plus* continuous variants, commodities → contract spec in the data, DEX → slippage from reserves.
Store contract/instrument metadata in the dataset, not the docs.
Buy commoditized history and crosswalks; build everything that encodes your assumptions.
Version data, never overwrite. Fail loudly on validation violations.
Default storage stack is partitioned Parquet + DuckDB/Polars. Escalate only on concurrency, governance, or latency pressure.
Backtests that assume fills at the close mis-model price formation, not just costs. Model spread, depth, and queue explicitly.
Liquidity is three things (spread/depth/resiliency); check the one your strategy actually needs.
Intraday seasonality is a confounder before it's a feature — the same signal means different things at different times of day.
Choose the feed level by what your signal *requires*; L1 signals are crowded precisely because L1 is cheap.
Midprice for signal measurement, executable prices for PnL. Report both markouts; the gap is the tradability test.
Reconstruction is accounting — enforce invariants and fail fast; a venue-local book is not the market.
**Dollar bars are the default.** Information bars only when order-flow dynamics are the object of study.
Information bars are gated by trade-classification accuracy: Lee-Ready ~95% vs. tick test ~80%. Reconstruct the book to get quotes if you need imbalance bars.
Watch for the threshold spiral in adaptive imbalance bars; fixed thresholds in production.
Use jump-robust local volatility (Lee–Mykland) rather than daily-σ thresholds — the naive rule fails in both directions depending on the day.
Flag and exclude; never interpolate ticks and quotes.
Sequence numbers over timestamps for ordering, when both exist.
Nulls in a continuously-sessionized panel may mean "no activity," not "missing data." Check before aggregating.
Every fact carries two timestamps: the period it describes and when that version became observable.
Conservative default for equities: use filing acceptance as availability; track the earlier 8-K separately only if event precision matters.
Crypto needs a **confirmation policy** in the PIT contract — block time alone permits reorg lookahead.
Never interpolate macro series onto a decision grid.
Store the *published* release timestamp; schedules shift.
Identifier match ≠ correct resolution. Pick the layer (entity / security / contract) explicitly.
Precision over recall in entity matching; the failure is asymmetric.
All joins constrained by both availability time and identifier effective-date range.
Detect leakage by running as-known vs. latest-available and comparing.
Legal and PIT integrity are hard gates; score comparisons happen only after.
For text: accession number as key, `accepted_at` for timing, store raw + cleaned + extraction metadata.
Synthetic data is a robustness tool, not evidence. Real held-out data is the arbiter.
Fix the generator before strategy selection; otherwise you overfit to its biases.
Evaluate fidelity, utility, and privacy **separately** — each can pass while another fails badly.
Marginal-distribution tests are necessary and never sufficient; test dependence and temporal structure independently.
ACF of squared returns is the cheapest high-value diagnostic for volatility clustering.
Beat the classical baseline (stationary bootstrap, GARCH) before accepting a deep generator.
Never treat generated data as evidence about scenarios outside the training support.
Regime-conditioned generation inherits the regime detector's errors.

**Freeze the evaluation environment before optimizing anything in it.** Attribution of a performance delta to a design change is only valid if everything else is versioned and recorded.

**Separate feasibility from durability.** A credible story with an infeasible implementation is not a strategy; a feasible implementation with no story is a backtest whose failures are uninterpretable.
**Prefer edges grounded in constraints over edges grounded in information.** Information edges erode on replication; constraint and risk-tolerance edges survive publicity.
**Distinguish mechanics from parameters.** Mechanics changes bump the version and reset the baseline; parameter changes don't.
**Use three metric layers with distinct roles** and never let end-to-end economics drive micro-decisions during development.
**Test admissibility with one question:** at decision time *t*, were the features computable and was the label already resolved?
**Count buffers in trading days, never calendar days.**
**Seal the holdout and open it once,** after the whole pipeline — including mapping and cost assumptions — is frozen.
**Run cadence feasibility before signal research.** If costs dominate at the intended horizon, no signal quality rescues it.
**Make search countable.** Trial counts are an input to overfitting corrections, not paperwork.
**When a preflight check fails, revise the setup, don't engineer around it.**
**Treat a published anomaly as a hypothesis, not evidence.** Independent validation must happen inside your own setup and cost assumptions.
**Define the label before selecting an algorithm.** Label misalignment manufactures predictability that no model choice can fix.
**Match the execution convention to the actual execution assumption** and keep it identical in label computation and backtest PnL — the gap is 50–100 bps per trade on daily equities.
**Any step estimating parameters from data is fit train-only, refit per fold.** When unsure, treat it as fitted.
**Preserve tails when tails are the prediction target;** winsorize only when they aren't.
**Treat missingness as three distinct mechanisms** and never let imputation erase it without an indicator.
**Compute standard errors on effective sample size, not row count.** Overlap can shrink 248k observations to 12k.
**Summarize diagnostics by fold, never pooled.** Sign consistency across folds is the stability gate; pooled IC can read 0.001 while fold-level reads 0.064.
**Thresholds set both event magnitude and base rate simultaneously** — choose them against the turnover and cost budget, and estimate percentiles within-fold.
**Log the searched-set size with every p-value.** Without it, significance claims are uninterpretable.
**Separate the exploration pass from the confirmation pass,** and never confirm on the data used to promote.
**Post-hoc parameter changes are new trials.** Count them.
**Assign a causal role (confounder / mediator / collider) before conditioning on any variable.** More controls is not safer — conditioning on a collider fabricates correlation.
**A gross spread that doesn't clear estimated costs is a stop, not a revise.**
**Expect most candidates to fail correction.** Zero of 13 surviving BH-FDR is a normal result, not a broken pipeline.
**Separate meaning-changing choices from noise-reduction choices.** The first create new hypotheses and new trials; the second trade variance for bias within one hypothesis.
**If you cannot name the economic mechanism, you have a data pattern.** Hold it to a higher evidentiary standard or drop it.
**Classify every feature as signal or state before evaluating it.** State variables legitimately show weak marginal association and only earn their place through interactions.
**Match lookback, cadence, and smoothing to the label horizon.** Horizon mismatch is the most common source of unstable estimates.
**Use range-based estimators for variance and ATR for sizing** — they answer different questions.
**Test delay sensitivity before optimizing any flow-based feature.** Contemporaneous correlation routinely exceeds lagged by an order of magnitude.
**The anchor, the peer set, and the maturity pair *are* the hypothesis.** Changing them is not tuning.
**Verify venue-specific clocks** (funding intervals, roll schedules, session boundaries) rather than assuming the common convention.
**Repeating slow data across fast rows inflates N without adding information.** Weight by uniqueness.
**Encode event proximity and phase, never event outcomes,** in pre-event windows.
**Breadth beats marginal IC.** A slightly better signal on a small universe loses to a thin signal on a large one.
**Deduplicate within families before the model stage,** and prefer fold stability over single-metric wins when picking cluster representatives.
**Every interaction is a separate trial** and enters the multiple-testing budget — 5 × 3 × 3 is 45 tests, not one experiment.
**Demand the right event-time shape, not just a significant average.** Correct sign, correct timing, correct asymmetry.
**Log fitted parameters and training windows for any feature that depends on a fitted object.**
**A fitted object is a feature generator with an estimation window attached.** Refit inside the training fold, version the parameters, log the window.
**Always use filtered output, never smoothed.** Smoothed states and full-sample posteriors borrow from the future.
**Model selection is a fitted step.** ARIMA order, HMM state count, fractional *d* — all must be re-selected within each training window.
**Diagnostics are features.** Rolling ADF/KPSS statistics, CUSUM values, and time-since-break are conditioning variables, not just gates.
**Take the smallest differencing order that achieves stationarity,** preserving maximum memory — and record the boundary convention as part of the definition.
**Prefer methods that separate direction, surprise, and confidence** over methods that collapse them into one smoothed line.
**Compute spectral features causally on trailing windows,** and remember window length sets frequency resolution.
**Treat non-causal transforms (wavelets) as horizon-discovery diagnostics,** then build causal proxies at the discovered scale.
**Time-augment path signatures** or ordering information is lost; default to depth-2 log-signatures.
**HAR is the strongest simple volatility baseline** — roughly half the out-of-sample RMSE of GARCH on index data.
**Guard parameter-derived features against their own validity conditions** — long-run variance is meaningless under IGARCH.
**Separate refit cadence from between-refit update logic.** Most recursions update daily on fixed parameters.
**Uncertainty is a feature even when the point estimate is already included.** Identical forecasts with different interval widths are different states.
**Relabel latent states by a stable characteristic across refits,** or the feature is incoherent over time.
**Feed regime probabilities as continuous inputs rather than hard-switching between models** — inference is least certain exactly at the transitions that matter.
**Compute temporal features first, then apply the panel layer.** Never the reverse.

**Keep the set compact.** One or two volatility features, one regime feature, one signal-transform feature, and a limited set of cross-sectional transforms are usually enough to establish what fitted methods add over Ch. 8 directs.
**The timestamp contract, not the model, decides whether a text feature is tradable.** Publication ≠ scrape ≠ vendor timestamp; pick the one you could have acted on.
**Verify the model's training cutoff predates the backtest period** — for the encoder, the topic model, and every other fitted component.
**Always run the TF-IDF baseline.** Failure to beat it points at labels, alignment, or task definition rather than capacity.
**Benchmark accuracy does not transfer across text distributions.** Run a cross-dataset evaluation; expect drops of tens of points when label conventions differ.
**"FinBERT" names several incompatible checkpoints.** Match corpus *and* label definition to your task.
**Snapshot documents at first availability and reject revisions by default.**
**Deduplicate syndicated and revised content within (ticker, date)** before aggregation, or you count the same information many times.
**Sizing the purge gap is a function of the signal's decay horizon,** not a fixed constant.
**Pin embedding model versions and key caches by document hash + model ID.** Vector meaning changes when models change.
**Chunk within documents, never across them,** and never fit global transforms on the full corpus.
**Coverage is endogenous** — evaluate IC conditional on coverage, and consider modeling coverage as its own signal.
**Test the signal against a realistic availability delay.** IC that dies with a one-hour lag is a speed edge, not an information edge.
**Attention weights are routing, not explanation.**
**Prefer abstention to a low-confidence record,** and validate at the pipeline boundary.
**Separate extraction from aggregation** so models can be upgraded without rebuilding feature history.

**Reserve LLMs for ambiguous, rare, or schema-rich tasks;** high-volume daily features should use encoders or distilled models unless the LLM adds measurable value after latency, cost, and validation constraints.
**Unbiasedness is not a goal for prediction.** Trading bias for variance lowers MSE when p is large relative to n and signal-to-noise is low.
**Match the penalty to the signal's structure.** Diffuse and correlated → Ridge. Genuinely sparse → LASSO. Correlated clusters → Elastic Net.
**Optimize the stability ratio, not the mean.** Most of the achievable gain comes from variance reduction across folds.
**Calibrate the hyperparameter search range to the estimator's loss convention and sample size,** or you will search only the near-OLS region and conclude regularization does nothing.
**Use nested walk-forward whenever signal is weak.** Single-loop selection bias can flip the reported sign.
**Report trial count, search space, selected configuration, and fold-level dispersion** with every tuned result.
**Winsorize before standardizing, and fit both on training data only.** Both errors fail silently.
**Report turnover alongside every statistical metric.** No statistical metric measures tradability.
**Report effective sample size whenever weights are applied,** and verify the reweighted set spans multiple regimes.
**Choose regression vs. classification from the score-to-position mapping,** not from preference — they encode different information.
**Calibrate probabilities only if position size depends on probability levels.** Rank-based mappings don't need it.
**Treat AUC above 0.65 out-of-sample as a leakage alarm,** not a success.
**Use SHAP for descriptive attribution, never causal claims,** and bootstrap within fold to separate regime shift from estimation noise.
**Flag single-feature-dominated predictions** for review or size reduction — concentrated attribution is fragility.
**Conformal coverage in finance is empirical, not guaranteed.** Monitor by fold, regime, magnitude bucket, and asset characteristic; a marginal number hides the failures that matter.
**Diagnose undercoverage before switching methods** — leakage, window size, and score definition are more common causes than exchangeability.
**A significant IC on a huge sample is not a strong signal.** Separate statistical from economic significance every time.
**Check sign stability before concluding a flat IC means an unstable model.** Usually the features simply carry no ranking content.
**Every later model must beat this baseline.** A gradient-boosting model that underperforms Ridge has added complexity without adding predictive power.
**Choose the GBM library on operational criteria** — training throughput, inference latency, categorical leakage safety, ecosystem — because post-tuning accuracy differences are noise.
**Verify GPU actually helps before assuming it does.** Precision support and dataset scale can make GPU slower than CPU.
**Match the objective to where trading occurs.** Rank objectives pay in high-breadth cross-sections where only tails trade; they cost calibration you may need downstream.
**Use monotonic constraints as theory-driven regularization,** and verify via constrained-vs-unconstrained SHAP dependence that they cost no IC.
**Tune regularization before tree structure.** It has the larger out-of-sample effect in low-SNR regimes.
**Cap trial budgets at 50–100.** More trials find validation noise, and that is the most common backtest-to-live failure.
**Try multi-objective search even when you only care about one objective** — constraining a second can reach parameter regions single-objective search misses.
**Prefer TreeSHAP to native importance for any decision,** and use exact interaction values to detect mechanisms that shift by regime beneath a stable-looking average.
**Monitor SHAP drift as a leading indicator,** but confirm with outcome metrics before acting.
**Cross-validate explanations across model families.** Equal-accuracy models disagree; agreement across architectures is the stronger evidence.
**Discount tabular benchmarks that assume IID splits.** Attention-heavy architectures degrade fastest under exactly the temporal shift finance has.
**Audit retrieval-augmented models for temporal isolation** before believing any reported number.
**Flexibility extends signal; it does not create it.** Where the linear baseline is flat, expect the interval to stay on zero.
**Loss function choice can dominate depth.** On heavy-tailed targets, MAE's refusal to chase extremes is worth more than extra capacity.
**Treat early stopping as a tuned outcome** — the optimal tree count varied by 10× across case studies.
**Define the target before choosing the architecture.** Recursive forecasting, multi-horizon path forecasting, horizon-label prediction, and direct allocation are four different problems.
**For cross-sectional ranking, predict the label directly** — it matches the evaluation metric and avoids compounding.
**A forecasting-native architecture is a liability on a ranking label.** Sophisticated path-forecasting inductive biases actively hurt when only the horizon label is scored.
**Library choice is a modeling choice.** Forecasting frameworks impose the path formulation.
**Clear D-Linear before believing anything more complex.**
**Test whether shuffling the input degrades the model.** If it doesn't, the model isn't using temporal structure.
**Compare families with a paired daily-difference interval,** not two separate confidence intervals — clearing zero and beating the baseline are different claims.
**Longer lookbacks add noise more reliably than they add signal** in weak, non-stationary series.
**Never trust a single-split IC at this SNR.** Rerun noise can exceed the effect being measured.
**Zero-shot foundation models on returns are worse than random.** Domain pretraining or fine-tuning is required, not optional.
**Treat the pretraining corpus as a leakage channel** and verify temporal separation from the evaluation period.
**Report the accuracy-efficiency frontier, not parameter count.** Scaling laws don't hold here.
**TSFMs are credible for volatility and VaR, not returns** — the target structure transfers where the return signal does not.
**Always conformally calibrate deep-model intervals.** Raw Gaussian intervals under-cover by an order of magnitude.
**Ranking credibility and uncertainty reliability are independent properties.** Check both before sizing on a signal.
**Make early stopping a per-case-study outcome** — high-frequency panels peak early, longer-horizon panels keep climbing.
**A large sample size triggers model comparison, not model replacement.**
**Name the objective before choosing the method.** Variance explained, variance plus pricing error, and pricing error alone select different factors.
**A factor that explains covariation is not necessarily priced.** Attribution factors and priced factors are different objects with different uses.
**Check N/T against the BBP threshold before trusting any component.** Below it, no technique recovers the factor.
**Prefer idiosyncratic-volatility normalization to correlation PCA** — it removes noise without flattening genuine differences in common-factor exposure.
**Apply shrinkage before PCA on large cross-sections,** and prefer eigenvalue shrinkage to scree-plot inspection when N/T is moderate.
**Measure eigenvector stability with cosine similarity and apply Procrustes rotation when eigenvalues cluster.** Unstable loadings generate phantom turnover that costs real money.
**Separate fast volatility dynamics from slow correlation dynamics** with different half-lives in production risk models.
**Interpret higher-order components descriptively, never structurally** — they rotate across regimes.
**Regress loadings on observable characteristics** to test whether a "latent" factor is a known factor renamed.
**Lag characteristics relative to returns and impute rather than drop** — missingness is informative about firm size.
**Report a range of K, not a single optimum.** The out-of-sample selection rule is sensitive to the test-asset set.
**Test assets are a design choice.** Report how conclusions change when the span is enriched.
**Never select a factor model on reconstruction loss.** Good contemporaneous fit is compatible with useless forecasts.
**Use the adapter's separability** — swap Stage 2 forecasters without retraining Stage 1.
**Where N/T is unfavorable, prefer models that map characteristics to loadings** over models that estimate loadings from returns.
**Adversarial objectives discipline against worst cases; reconstruction objectives discipline against averages.** Choose based on which failure you care about.
**Report gross and net, with and without microcaps.** Characteristic predictability concentrates exactly where it is least tradable.
**Read model disagreement as model risk, not as a tie to be broken** — differing rank correlations across objectives are informative in themselves.
**Identification precedes estimation.** No estimator rescues a design that cannot justify a causal interpretation.
**Write the DAG before choosing the method,** and let structure — not significance or feature importance — determine the adjustment set.
**More controls is not safer.** Mediators change the estimand, colliders open closed paths, treatment descendants introduce post-treatment bias.
**Timing discipline is necessary but insufficient** — a pre-treatment variable can still be a collider or selection variable.
**Start with the treatment–outcome pair, not the estimator.** Mechanism-adjacent outcomes support more credible claims than broad market outcomes.
**Declare the estimand precisely,** including horizon — different horizons are different causal questions, not robustness checks.
**Distinguish subgroup ATEs from CATEs, and confounders from effect modifiers.** Both distinctions change what is being estimated.
**Cross-fit on expanding or rolling windows with a temporal gap,** never random folds.
**Sweep nuisance learners and treat large variation as instability,** not as a menu to pick from.
**Report the naive-vs-orthogonalized gap.** It is often above 50%, and it can run in either direction.
**Size permutation blocks to the autocorrelation.** Too-short blocks understate the null and inflate apparent significance.
**Run placebo dates before believing any event study,** and reject the design if the false-positive rate is high — no individual finding survives a broken design.
**Test every control as a target for spillover, per event.** For macro events, truly unaffected controls may not exist.
**A cumulative-effect credible interval is the diagnostic; a fraction of positive rows is not a posterior probability.**
**Treat discovered edges as hypotheses.** Method outputs on identical data ranged from 1 to 42 edges.
**Weight edges by cross-method agreement and effect magnitude,** not by p-value or by any single implementation.
**Causal analysis reduces out-of-sample degradation when heterogeneity carries information; it does not manufacture alpha when the signal inverts.**
**Causal credibility and predictive signal are separable in both directions** — neither licenses the other.
**Treat a good equity curve as a claim to attack, not a result to confirm.** Failed tests are the main product.
**Default to disbelief.** With a low prior on edge, false positives can outnumber true ones.
**Record the protocol before interpreting results** — timing, rebalance, sizing, fills, constraints, costs.
**Separate signal computation from execution in time.** Same-bar execution fuses past and future.
**Choose vectorized vs. event-driven on semantics, not aesthetics.** The question is whether strategy behavior depends on simulated state.
**Treat engine defaults as assumptions** — order sequencing, cash release, share granularity, and missing-data policy all change the path.
**Build an unflattering baseline first,** and use large deviations from it as an infrastructure-bug signal in both directions.
**Report gross and net together.** The gap reveals whether performance comes from forecasting or is consumed by trading.
**Compute break-even cost and compare it to the assumed cost.** Proximity is fragility regardless of headline Sharpe.
**Never read max drawdown as a standalone quality measure** — it is an extreme statistic that grows with sample length.
**Check whether holding period matches signal horizon.** A mismatch requires explanation.
**Build regime labels point-in-time with expanding medians.** A full-sample threshold contaminates the diagnostic.
**Weight conditional metrics by slice size,** and report observation counts alongside every regime statistic.
**Report all standard regimes including the unfavorable ones,** and pre-specify definitions to avoid regime snooping.
**Ask whether regime dependence is intentional and compensated,** not merely whether it exists.
**Adjust Sharpe inference for serial dependence** before annualizing or testing.
**Count effective, not nominal, trials** — adjacent parameter values are neither independent nor identical.
**Keep exploration and confirmation separate,** and confirm on data that did not guide the specification.
**Read the screening-prior table as a scrutiny trigger, not a threshold.** A Sharpe above 2.0 on a diversified strategy is a reason to look harder, not to celebrate.
**The allocator is a model.** Specify its objective, inputs, constraints, and evaluation before implementing an optimizer.
**Constraints are part of the estimator.** They regularize the mapping from noisy inputs to weights, and each has a robustness reading.
**Effective breadth, not nominal breadth, drives realized IR.** Correlated positions are not independent bets.
**Read IC as R².** An IC of 0.03 explains ~0.09% of cross-sectional variance — value comes from repetition, not single-name predictability.
**Match estimation-window horizons to signal horizons deliberately,** not by default settings.
**Treat allocator hyperparameters as tunable parameters requiring out-of-sample validation.** Holding the forecast model fixed does not protect against fitting the allocator to the answer key.
**Check risk contribution, not just capital concentration.** Equal capital weights ≠ equal risk contributions.
**Judge covariance models by the portfolios they generate,** not by matrix-fit metrics.
**Clear equal weight before taking any allocator seriously.** Estimation error often overwhelms the theoretical gains from optimization.
**Alpha ranking matters more than alpha calibration.** Scale error is absorbed by leverage; ranking error is not.
**Hedge in proportion to the reliability of the exposure estimate.** Full neutralization on a noisy beta can raise realized variance.
**Volatility-match the short leg** rather than equal-notional dollar neutrality.
**Treat full Kelly as an upper bound.** Raw Kelly implies 30×+ leverage on real data.
**Expect narrow allocator spreads.** Best-to-worst of 0.12 Sharpe against a cost channel that moved returns from +46.6% to +1.5%.
**Allocator optimization helps most where signal is strongest** — and cannot rescue a weak signal-cost combination.
**Pool the Sharpe across the universe when training end-to-end,** and use a two-pass gradient because Sharpe is non-separable across mini-batches.
**Report the cost-stress curve, not the gross number.** Gross parity with heuristics can vanish entirely by 20 bp.
**Make seed variance a reported metric for learned allocators.**
**Respect closing calendars in cross-sectional attention** — asynchronous closes are a lookahead channel.
**Model costs from feature evaluation onward, not as a final haircut.** Turnover and IC must be judged together.
**There is no universal cost number.** Routing, urgency, and execution style determine whether an edge survives — TAQ-based estimates and zero-cost assumptions err in opposite directions.
**Model financing, borrow, and transaction taxes explicitly.** They are the costs most often omitted and can exceed the spread.
**Separate temporary from permanent impact** — only the temporary component responds to scheduling and venue choice.
**Capacity depends on who else is trading the idea.** It is not a static property of the signal.
**Match model complexity to participation:** spread below 0.5% ADV, linear to 2%, square-root above.
**Use the upper end of published impact-coefficient ranges when calibrating from priors,** and the stressed parameters when the regime is ambiguous.
**Backtest with contemporaneous regime costs** so crisis periods pay crisis prices.
**Replace notional-bps whenever traded price and notional exposure are not proportional** — options are the canonical case.
**Execution algorithms trade impact against timing risk; they do not remove cost.** Tie urgency to alpha decay.
**Generate execution schedules under multiple scenarios.** Wide trajectory variation means the trade is fragile to miscalibration.
**Decompose implementation shortfall before acting on it,** and always ask whether the cost was market-driven or execution-driven.
**Condition TCA on regime,** or the comparison set is unfair in both directions.
**Read TCA residual structure as a specification diagnostic:** regime-specific residuals mean missing conditioning; size-specific residuals mean a misspecified impact function.
**Test how much turnover your risk model creates with the signal held fixed.** Covariance churn is trades with no informational content.
**Rank signals by alpha-to-go, not raw IC.** A fast signal with high impact cost can be worthless by the time the position is built.
**Compute break-even turnover and minimum required edge both ways;** disagreement means one of the inputs is wrong.
**State capacity as a function of AUM and a Sharpe threshold,** and remember turnover, not participation alone, converts flow limits into capital limits.
**Precommit kill criteria before deployment.**
**Try the repair ladder before abandoning** — turnover, execution, universe, capacity — but drop the strategy if net performance stays unacceptable.
**Run both fixed and relative cost regimes.** Disagreement diagnoses the cost model, not the signal.
**Build every adaptive control from information available at decision time,** and treat model-inferred regimes as a leakage channel unless the state path is never re-estimated.
**A control that cannot be specified ex ante and reconstructed afterward is not a valid control.**
**Variance is the highest moment you can usually estimate.** Treat skewness, kurtosis, and deep quantiles as requiring stronger assumptions or much more data.
**Report VaR and CVaR together,** and prefer historical simulation as the base method — Cornish-Fisher destabilizes at high confidence under realistic kurtosis.
**Use the Cantelli bound as a distribution-free floor** when parametric methods are untrustworthy.
**Compute tail metrics by regime and present worst-regime CVaR prominently.** Unconditional estimates average over states that differ by ~2.7×.
**Apply liquidity haircuts to tail estimates** — the effect can be 50–100% of effective VaR.
**Evaluate volatility models with QLIKE for risk and variance-MSE for alpha.** Other loss functions reverse rankings depending on the proxy.
**Measure duration and recovery time, not just drawdown depth.** Investors redeem before recovery, and their realized return is worse than the strategy's.
**Distinguish gamma from delta drawdowns** — they call for different hedges.
**Report factor attribution with HAC confidence bands.** A contribution whose interval spans zero did not "drive" performance.
**Span every asset class held in the factor model,** or cross-asset exposures get misattributed to alpha.
**Check residual correlations and precision-matrix stability** before trusting a covariance model in an optimizer.
**Monitor exposures on a rolling basis.** Static loadings silently mis-size hedges as tilts drift.
**Stress costs alongside returns.** Historical replay alone understates execution damage in crisis.
**Map every discovered vulnerability to accepted risk, a hedge, reduced exposure, or a trigger** — and enforce it with a written memo.
**Run reverse stress tests,** which surface combinations forward scenarios miss.
**Pre-define regime thresholds** or the cap logic becomes an overfitted parameter.
**Calibrate stops from the strategy's own MAE/MFE excursions,** and judge them by realized exit behavior rather than headline drawdown.
**Use learned exits to size winners, not to replace stops on losers.**
**Wrap learned policies in hard deterministic envelopes.**
**Prefer graduated escalation to a binary cutoff,** because mechanical drawdown rules can lock in losses that would have recovered.
**Give every kill switch a metric, threshold, action, escalation path, and reinstatement condition.**
**Use RL where the action is the optimization target and the reward is directly measurable** — not for generic alpha discovery.
**"Model-free" describes the algorithm, not the modeling burden.** State design, reward shaping, and simulator construction carry the assumptions.
**Reward engineering, not algorithm choice, determines whether the learned policy matches the financial objective.**
**Include regime indicators in the state** and the policy becomes regime-conditioned without explicit switching logic.
**Never let hard constraints depend on learned behavior.**
**Choose on-policy vs. off-policy on the stability-efficiency trade:** cheap simulator data favors SAC; scarce historical data favors PPO.
**Use distributional RL when risk preferences may change** — it makes them configurable without retraining.
**Treat seed variation as a policy-character question, not just a performance variance question.** The same reward can produce uniform, back-loaded, or oscillating policies across seeds.
**Constrain the action space and penalize deviation from a reference schedule** to keep execution agents economically coherent.
**A simulator without queue priority, partial fills, impact, and latency will teach the agent to exploit assumptions that do not survive contact with live markets.**
**Inspect policy *shape* against the analytical benchmark before comparing performance** — inventory-responsive quoting is the diagnostic, not one episode's PnL.
**Require matched accounting and a friction-aware benchmark set** before claiming a learned hedge beats delta hedging.
**Prefer IRL to behavior cloning when the environment may change,** since cloning copies actions rather than objectives.
**Read inferred rewards qualitatively.** The feature basis constrains what objectives can be expressed.
**Randomize the domain rather than calibrating one "correct" environment.**
**Check participation rate before believing any strategy result.** Above roughly one day's volume, strong impact assumptions flip essentially every paper winner into a loser.
**Run offline policy evaluation before any capital,** and define go/no-go criteria before staged scaling.
**Treat grounding as architecture, not prompting.** Post-hoc fact-checking neither scales nor addresses the cause.
**Ingestion errors are irreversible downstream.** Validate parser output on representative documents before trusting it at scale.
**Tune chunk size as a hyperparameter** on an evaluation grid, and use parent-document retrieval to get precision and context together.
**Track publication date, fiscal period, and ingestion timestamp separately.** Filtering by period labels alone leaks information into backtests.
**Record structural role and extraction method per chunk,** or citations can look precise while failing claim-evidence alignment.
**Benchmark embeddings on your own corpus and query mix.** Cross-model spread can be no larger than within-model variation across query types.
**Combine semantic and lexical retrieval.** Pure vector search fails on tickers, codes, and quoted figures.
**Verify rerankers on financial passages before adopting them** — a generic cross-encoder degraded MRR by 36% in the chapter's test.
**Pre-filter on metadata before ANN search,** never post-filter.
**Prefer focused retrieval to long context,** and benchmark positional effects on the target model.
**Never trust a citation without verifying it.** Semantic similarity between claim and cited text is a cheap check.
**Delegate arithmetic to code.** Computation failure is invisible to faithfulness metrics because the evidence is correct.
**Diagnose which of the five failure modes is binding before changing anything.**
**Score abstention quality as a first-class metric,** and include unanswerable queries in the evaluation set.
**Put security in the accuracy harness** so robustness regressions surface like accuracy regressions.
**Choose RAG for evidence-grounded analysis over changing documents; choose fine-tuning for a repeatable skill over stable labels.**
**Version the whole stack together** — corpus, embedder, reranker, prompts, generator — and persist a retrieval bundle per response.
**Use an agent only when the question genuinely requires multi-tool orchestration.**
**Restate the question as a path pattern before building a graph.** If it doesn't decompose into relationship chains, use simpler tools.
**Never encode entity attributes as relationships.** It complicates queries without adding relational insight.
**Treat average node degree below 2–3 as an extraction problem, not a domain property.**
**Define the schema before extraction,** so the model emits graph-ready objects rather than text requiring cleanup.
**Separate mentions from identities,** key on stable identifiers, and treat corporate actions as first-class identity-updating events.
**Store evidence with the edge.** A relationship without source context cannot be verified or corrected.
**Make extraction idempotent** — reprocessing must update the same record, not create a parallel copy that inflates path counts.
**Monitor schema validity, provenance coverage, duplicate-node rate, and temporal consistency** — standard NLP metrics hide these regressions.
**Maintain a frozen gold subset** and regression-test extraction across prompt and model changes.
**Prefer parameterized query templates with an LLM router to free-form Cypher generation** in audited deployments.
**Make query safety architectural, not optional:** read-only credentials, allowlisted schema, parameterization, execution limits, query logging.
**Cite two layers — the graph row and the underlying disclosure text.**
**Use multiple centrality measures as separate features** rather than picking one.
**Cross-graph interaction features are the distinctive payoff,** because they encode dependencies factor models assume away.
**Trust topology metrics from stated relationships more than from estimated correlations,** and match the network filter to the analytical goal.
**Start with hand-crafted graph features; add learned representations only on out-of-sample evidence after costs.**
**Gate everything on disclosure time,** and split, embargo, and filter accordingly.
**Recompute derived relationships on the same cadence as the underlying data,** and treat them as artifacts rather than disclosures.
**Log snapshot hash and extractor version** so historical feature values can be replayed.
**Keep the relationship vocabulary to ~8–15 types** and defer ontology alignment until integration requires it.
**Keep agents read-only unless the use case demands side effects.** Read-only systems are easier to secure and evaluate, and match every credible public prototype.
**Use agents only for evidence-rich tasks.** With stable structured labels, the adaptive loop adds latency and non-determinism without accuracy.
**Start with ReAct; add ToT only for branch-heavy decisions; add Reflexion only once evaluation can identify which lessons are worth keeping.**
**Give every persisted lesson a validity horizon,** or Reflexion converts temporary heuristics into durable blind spots.
**Cap the reasoning budget** and return bounded output with explicit uncertainty when exhausted.
**Use typed state objects, not chat history.** Transcripts cannot be queried for the evidence behind a specific estimate.
**Checkpoint at decision boundaries, not intervals.**
**Replay by freezing tool outputs and varying only prompts or policies,** or you will mistake evidence drift for prompt improvements.
**Tool quality sets the ceiling prompt quality cannot raise.** Debug tool contracts and parsing before prompt wording.
**Write tool descriptions with explicit negative guidance** — when *not* to call.
**Expose only phase-relevant state, tools, and sources at each step.**
**Enforce cutoffs at the tool boundary, never in the model narrative.**
**Prefer structured abstention to unstructured fallback** when the schema cannot be satisfied.
**Choose frameworks on state visibility, replay, and policy enforcement,** not benchmarks.
**Prove the single-agent baseline before adding agents,** against explicit acceptance criteria.
**Read forecast spread as a property of the question.** Uniform outputs across agents are the bug; similar outputs on one-directional evidence are not.
**Make aggregation and calibration explicit, disjoint, and versioned** — extremizing then Platt-scaling compounds overconfidence.
**Monitor sharpness alongside ECE.** Improved calibration with collapsed sharpness is not improvement.
**Treat search-retrieved post-cutoff evidence as the dominant contamination risk** on resolved panels, and let contamination analysis override demo performance.
**Apply a retention rubric to every component** and remove those that fail it.
**Keep methodology in libraries and a retrievable skills corpus, not in the agent prompt.** The prompt stays short and stable; the corpus grows.
**Separate engineering and research observability views.**
**Version prompts, corpora, and models as regulated artifacts.**
**Cascade models by phase and measure per-phase error rates,** never assuming the saving.
**Reuse existing governance artifacts (the IPS) as the agent's operational boundary** rather than inventing new ones.
**Test security adversarially with specified expected allow/deny behavior and required log fields** — converting posture from narrative assurance to measurable behavior.
**Separate technical divergence from statistical decay before diagnosing anything.** Until parity is verified, live deviations could be either, making diagnosis impossible.
**Run the same source files in both modes.** Rewriting for production creates two implementations and two places for bugs to hide.
**Make signal generation deterministic** — no system time, no run-varying seeds, no environment-dependent external state.
**Detect stale connectivity actively with a heartbeat,** and reconcile broker state on every reconnect before resuming trading.
**Treat broker routing as an execution-quality decision.** Cost dispersion across brokers dwarfs commission differences, and PFOF explains little of it.
**Use client order IDs as idempotency keys** so crashes and timeouts cannot produce duplicates.
**Model orders as an explicit state machine that tolerates out-of-order messages** and records race resolutions in the audit trail.
**Never blindly retry rejections** — the cause determines the correct response.
**Halt on reconciliation discrepancies rather than auto-correcting,** or record-keeping errors become trading errors.
**Verify parity stage by stage** so divergence can be binary-searched rather than guessed at.
**Make parity tests fail loudly on a missing live pipeline** rather than silently passing against an empty log.
**Match training and inference venues,** and when impossible, measure and document the convention differences as an explicit verification task.
**Source warm-up data from the executing session,** not a research-time loader, or rankings and sizing run on stale prices.
**Persist kill-switch state across restarts** — an unlatched switch after a crash re-enables trading at the worst moment.
**Reject orders on stale data** using a per-asset freshness timestamp.
**Refuse to start a trading cycle on a non-clean startup reconciliation.**
**Keep the kill switch independent of the component it controls,** and make each level a single tested action.
**Encode the training-cutoff invariant explicitly** and persist both cutoff dates for later audit.
**Partition basket disposition into intended / attempted / accepted / failed** rather than a single status string.
**Run paper and live in parallel during transition** — the divergence is more diagnostic than either book's PnL.
**Verify legality, automated access, taxes, and margin rules in the target jurisdiction before building,** not after.
**Classify the failure before responding.** Same inputs → different outputs is a bug; same outputs → poor returns is decay.
**Validate data at ingest with a fail-closed policy on execution-critical feeds.** Most apparent drift is a silent data defect.
**Compute metrics on rolling windows across several lengths,** because point-in-time aggregates hide trends and multi-window agreement distinguishes noise from decay.
**Decompose Sharpe into hit rate and win/loss** — the two move differently and point to different causes.
**Track the backtest-to-live realization ratio over time,** not just absolute performance.
**Monitor execution quality alongside model metrics.** Cost inflation looks like model decay and retraining is the wrong fix.
**Calibrate alert thresholds from historical degradation episodes,** and delete any threshold that fires without changing a decision.
**Use PSI for binned features and K-S for continuous ones,** and treat PSI spikes as leading indicators.
**Watch SHAP rank stability, not just magnitude** — a collapsing core-feature contribution is an early warning.
**Run ADWIN or DDM continuously on the prediction-error stream,** and monitor the detector's own alert frequency.
**Read the drift-vs-decay cross-tab.** Drift without decay means a robust model; decay without drift means your monitoring has gaps.
**Combine scheduled and triggered retraining** rather than choosing one.
**Shadow every candidate long enough to span multiple regimes,** with at least two rebalance cycles.
**Define a minimum effect size for promotion** and check statistical power before concluding the candidate is better.
**Phase capital in through explicit gates** — A/B testing with real money reveals illiquidity clustering and market impact that shadow mode cannot.
**Test the rollback mechanism before deploying the candidate.**
**Automate low-level rollbacks and require confirmation for performance-based ones.**
**Halt immediately on hard loss limits.** Do not wait for review; do not trade out of the hole.
**Restart gradually at reduced size after any breaker trip.**
**Time-limit and log every manual override.**
**Record a run manifest for every training run** so any deployed model traces to its exact inputs.
**Right-size the MLOps stack.** Monitoring and safety outrank tooling.
**Optimize for the process, not the strategy.** Individual models decay; a repeatable generate-test-deploy pipeline compounds.
**The systematic workflow is a bias-control mechanism first** — falsifiable hypotheses, out-of-sample testing, multiple-testing corrections.
**Choose the firm type as deliberately as the role.** It determines which skills you actually develop.
**Build T-shaped expertise,** because the boundary between alpha research and execution is dissolving.
**Read a few papers deeply rather than many shallowly.**
**Document failed experiments,** which carry more information than successes.
**Allocate frontier attention by time-to-return:** DeFi and AI governance now, quantum as monitoring only.
**Treat model governance as measurable risk,** not philosophy — interpretability, bias, robustness, auditability each have techniques and metrics.
**Apply every new technique to a real problem immediately,** or it never becomes expertise.
**Close gaps that complement existing strengths** rather than opening new skill tracks.
Optimize **gain expectancy under a survival constraint**, never terminal return. If a rule cannot lose the game, you have modeled the wrong game.
Treat prediction accuracy as a **weak lever**. Average win and average loss have far more range than win rate.
**Never add a filter without measuring its false-negative cost.** Over-filtering is the default failure mode of the competent.
Design for **cheap a posteriori exits**, not accurate a priori selection. The separation you want at entry does not exist.
Any system for an infinite game must be **stress tested, not optimized** — optimization tunes to a sample that will not repeat.
Assume the short book's weights drift adversely by construction; build the correction into the algorithm.
Simplicity is not a compromise. In complex systems, the robust heuristic usually outperforms the elaborate model.

**Model the frictions as first-class constraints**: borrow availability (3–5% of float), locate, uptick rule, SSR at −10%, jurisdictional bans. A backtest without them overstates short performance systematically.
**Build shorts around institutional liquidation flow**, not around fundamental doom. You are following size, not leading it.
**Exclude the squeeze geometry explicitly**: high short interest ∧ thin trading ∧ exhausted selling pressure. Crowded shorts are false positives (Ch. 1 §4).
**Never hold a short that requires no maintenance.** The structural short is a myth; every short position needs the same continuous risk process as a long — more, given the adverse weight drift.
**Prefer relative underperformance as the short thesis.** Sustainable, non-confrontational, and it is what the rest of the book is engineered around.
**Run the short book in bull markets too.** Skill decay is real, and downside protection is the product investors are actually paying for.
When a short becomes emotionally satisfying, **that is an exit signal**, not a conviction signal.
**Compute everything on the relative, currency-adjusted series** — OHLC, not just close. This is the substrate; every downstream module assumes it.
**Never mix series across sides.** The long book must mirror the short book's series and signals.
Choose `rebase=True` for development (memory) and rolling/`rebase=False` for tested production (lightweight, corporate-action-proof). Know which one you are running.
**Use `expanding().sum()` over `cumsum()`** for cumulative log returns; compute relative returns by subtracting benchmark log returns.
**Survivorship bias in a short backtest is conservative**, not disqualifying — you are testing against the fittest survivors.
**Treat valuation as sector- and regime-conditional.** Cheap PBR in machinery is a sell signal, not a buy.
Track **sector rotation**, not market tops and bottoms. Use `cyclicals − defensives` on the relative series; negative → defensive posture.
**Expensive or callable-only borrow is a long signal, not a short signal.**
Enter shorts on relative weakness early — the margin of safety matters more at the exit than the entry.
Relative stop levels are invisible to hunting algorithms but **require active management** to be fillable.
**Regime is triage, not forecasting.** Its job is to allocate research effort, not to predict.
**Use the same regime model on both sides.** Trend-following longs plus mean-reverting shorts is two contradictory models.
**Compute fractals on `mean(H, L, C)`, never on Close alone.** Close-based fractals land several bars off the true turn.
**Prefer parameter-free primitives.** Fractals port across timeframes and asset classes; RSI(14) and MACD(12,26) do not.
**Blend methods; do not crown one.** A weighted average of eight regime methods beats the best single one. Robustness comes from averaging, not from tuning weights.
**Weight lower fractal levels more heavily** (`{1:0.1, 2:0.4, 3:0.3, 4:0.2}`) — high levels lag badly at regime turns.
**Floor and ceiling only needs one condition** (a lower high, or a higher low) vs. three sequential conditions for higher-highs. It is more stable and it is the method of choice.
**Only two regimes.** Sideways is a pause inside a bull or bear context. Stability beats responsiveness for position management.
**In production, detect fractals by diffing the last row**, not by recomputing history.
**Choose your floor/ceiling baseline consciously**: `_chg` = nervous with many stops; fractal price = the production default with smaller sizes and lower risk appetite.
**The composite score is a sizing input**, not just a filter — multiply it into the position sizing algorithm for strength-adjusted sizing.
**Long-lookback breakouts need a time exit.** Halve size when a position has not made new extremes after half the duration.

rules.parent_title: The Trading Edge Is a Number, and Here Is the Formula
rules.text: **Report gain expectancy first.** Sharpe, Sortino, and friends are meaningless until expectancy is positive.

rules.parent_title: The Trading Edge Is a Number, and Here Is the Formula
rules.text: **Compute all three formulas** (arithmetic, geometric, Kelly) from the same three inputs. Use **partial Kelly (⅓–½)** in production.

rules.parent_title: The Trading Edge Is a Number, and Here Is the Formula
rules.text: **Decompose every improvement into signal vs. money management.** Know which module you are working on.

rules.parent_title: The Trading Edge Is a Number, and Here Is the Formula
rules.text: **Track two durations**: long for "does it make money over time," short for cyclicality → exposure allocation.

rules.parent_title: The Trading Edge Is a Number, and Here Is the Formula
rules.text: **Win rate is not the target.** A 30% win rate with right skew beats a 99% win rate with left skew.

rules.parent_title: The Trading Edge Is a Number, and Here Is the Formula
rules.text: **Match the risk metric to the skew**: trend following → **profit factor / gain-to-pain**; mean reversion → **tail ratio**.

rules.parent_title: The Trading Edge Is a Number, and Here Is the Formula
rules.text: **Shift signals forward one bar.** Always. Signal today, trade tomorrow.

rules.parent_title: The Trading Edge Is a Number, and Here Is the Formula
rules.text: **Short only in sideways or bear regimes**, and enter when a **bear-market rally rolls over** — not on breakdowns.

rules.parent_title: The Trading Edge Is a Number, and Here Is the Formula
rules.text: **Design the exit before the entry.** Bad exits are unrecoverable.

rules.parent_title: The Trading Edge Is a Number, and Here Is the Formula
rules.text: **Search pairs within sectors**, not across the universe. Require cointegration *and* ADF stationarity on both spread and ratio.

rules.parent_title: The Trading Edge Is a Number, and Here Is the Formula
rules.text: **In mean reversion, stationarity is the stop loss.** When it breaks, stop trading the pair.

rules.parent_title: The Trading Edge Is a Number, and Here Is the Formula
rules.text: **Moderate z-score thresholds beat extremes.** Enter ~1.7σ, exit ~1.2σ.

rules.parent_title: The Trading Edge Is a Number, and Here Is the Formula
rules.text: **Constrain evaluation windows to the period the relationship was tested on.**

rules.parent_title: Position Sizing: Money Is Made in the Money Management Module
rules.text: **Sizing beats picking.** Same signals + same universe + different sizing = different businesses. Optimize sizing before optimizing signals.

rules.parent_title: Position Sizing: Money Is Made in the Money Management Module
rules.text: **Every sizing algorithm = NAV allocation ÷ denominator.** Make both explicit; the denominator is where the design lives.

rules.parent_title: Position Sizing: Money Is Made in the Money Management Module
rules.text: **Round lots down, sign-preserving.** Naive rounding of negative share counts increases short risk.

rules.parent_title: Position Sizing: Money Is Made in the Money Management Module
rules.text: **Compute daily P&L on the existing position before resizing.** Doing it after is lookahead bias — check for this in any backtest you inherit.

rules.parent_title: Position Sizing: Money Is Made in the Money Management Module
rules.text: **Never average down.** It degrades three of four edge variables and its best case is breakeven.

rules.parent_title: Position Sizing: Money Is Made in the Money Management Module
rules.text: **Express conviction in units of risk**, never in units of feeling.

rules.parent_title: Position Sizing: Money Is Made in the Money Management Module
rules.text: **Never equal-weight.** Volatility ignored at the position level reappears at the portfolio level.

rules.parent_title: Position Sizing: Money Is Made in the Money Management Module
rules.text: **Cap single-trade risk at ~2%.** A ⅓ win rate implies routine 10-loss runs and 25-loss tails → 30–50% drawdowns at 2%.

rules.parent_title: Position Sizing: Money Is Made in the Money Management Module
rules.text: **Translate the annual vol budget to daily** (÷√252) and across names (÷√n).

rules.parent_title: Position Sizing: Money Is Made in the Money Management Module
rules.text: **Prefer ATR** among volatility measures — most stable, lowest readings; but expect higher gross exposure and turnover.

rules.parent_title: Position Sizing: Money Is Made in the Money Management Module
rules.text: **Use rolling Kelly as a signal, not only as a size.** Its collapse to zero in trendless markets is the feature, not a bug.

rules.parent_title: Position Sizing: Money Is Made in the Money Management Module
rules.text: **Trade fractional Kelly.** Full Kelly's drawdowns are survivable mathematically and not psychologically.

rules.parent_title: Position Sizing: Money Is Made in the Money Management Module
rules.text: **Continuous resizing costs you the average price** (FIFO drags it toward the trend) and costs commissions. Budget for both.

rules.parent_title: Position Sizing: Money Is Made in the Money Management Module
rules.text: **Capacity is signaled by inertia**, not by a formula.

rules.parent_title: Position Sizing: Money Is Made in the Money Management Module
rules.text: **Net exposure is a property of the signal; gross exposure is a property of the sizing.** Do not confuse the two knobs.
**Judge short liquidity by the exit, never the entry.** Liquidity is thinner on the way out than the way in, structurally.
**Borrow utilization > 50% is a hard exclusion.** Not a caution — an exclusion.
**Crowded shorts are anti-hedges.** They outperform in pullbacks because there is no institutional long money left to sell.
**Expensive or callable-only borrow is a long signal** (Ch. 3 §7), not a short signal.
**High dividend yield is a short *source*, not a short deterrent** — the yield defers the decline, it does not prevent it.
**Never short a name doing buybacks.** You are fighting an unlimited, price-insensitive bid.
**Short liability for dividends is real.** Maintain a dividend calendar per short position.
**Rich valuation alone is never a short thesis.** The thesis is rich valuation + decelerating earnings momentum = multiples compression.
**Expensive PBR = investing cash flow financed by financing cash flow.** Never hold those long through a bear market.
**Let regime ask the question, let fundamentals answer it.** "Why is it going down?" beats "why should it go down?"
**Beta *momentum* beats beta *level*.** Rising beta → worse returns; falling beta → better returns. Both contradict CAPM.
**Size inversely to beta**, and understand that beta-neutral implies **negative** net exposure. Net exposure and net beta are different constraints.
Resample to month-end for beta — daily rolling beta costs a great deal of compute for no signal.
**Risk management is the business.** The four levers (gross, net, net beta, concentration) are the entire dashboard.
**Gross exposure is the accelerator and the brake.** Make it dynamic, not fixed.
**Drive gross with `risk_appetite()`** — measure drawdown from peak, normalize against tolerance, EWM-smooth, apply a response curve, scale into bands. Set tolerance at ~**40% of annual volatility**.
**Choose the response curve by market shape:** linear for trending, aggressive (convex) for sideways/bear-trap regimes, conservative (concave) when you want to stay defensive longer.
**Keep gross bands sane** — 50–100% multi-strategy, 40–60% single strategy. Deleveraging has market impact.
**Never lever a left-skewed strategy** because the win rate looks safe. That is how they die.
**Net exposure is a view, not a risk measure.** Always read it alongside net beta.
**Keep borrow utilization below 40%** at the portfolio level (Ch. 7 excludes names above 50% at the security level).
**Beware the two net-reduction cheats**: oversized short bets and index futures. Both cut net while leaving real risk intact.
**Bear-market target: negative net beta with neutral-to-positive net exposure.** Not negative net exposure — that buys alpha at the cost of violent volatility.
**Run structurally more names short than long** (net negative concentration). It is the only way to keep short-book volatility from driving the portfolio, and it is only possible on relative series.
**Cap the largest-to-smallest bet ratio at 2.5.** Below it, tracking error and AUM stability improve materially.
**Name count must scale with gross exposure** if the volatility target is fixed.
**Stay on main exchanges when risk is off.** The reverse trade (long blue chips / short speculation) does not execute.
**Write the mandate down**, including the skew of your return distribution.
**Define smoothness as drawdown depth × duration × frequency**, never as volatility or Sharpe.
**Simulate strategy returns, not asset prices.** Distribution shape is an emergent property of exit rules, not of the instrument.
**Model each strategy's failure mode explicitly** — single-day replace-mode jumps for left skew, block-replacement regimes for right skew — plus correlated portfolio-level shocks.
**Never let recent volatility drive allocation.** Left-skewed strategies are at their calmest immediately before failing.
**Do not penalize right-skewed strategies for drawdowns.** Drawdowns are the price of convexity.
**Among classic allocators, prefer equal weight.** Its naivety is a feature: it does not rebalance into failure.
**Derive position caps from failure geometry**: min(st_dd_tolerance/st_dd, lt_dd_tolerance/lt_dd) × (1 − corr) × (1 − liquidity haircut).
**Let upper bands sum above 1.** Elasticity that is *earned* — both strategies working, equity near highs, oscillator at peak — is not the same as an arbitrary leverage cap.
**Remove leverage faster than you add it.** Asymmetric response is the design goal.
**Boost the working strategy when its counterpart fails**, and turn the boost off when both work or both fail. Smooth it monthly.
**Path dependency requires recursion.** `equity[t-1]` must determine allocation at `t`; pre-fill arrays with NaN.
**Make max drawdown tolerance the single control parameter.** Leverage becomes a consequence, not an input.
**Read allocation scorecards in two columns**: comfort metrics (Sharpe, MaxDD, win rate) and robustness metrics (profit ratio, tail ratio, gain expectancy, common sense ratio). Optimize the second.
**A profit ratio below 1 with a high win rate is the left-skew trap.** Check both together, always.
**Log missed trades and overrides, not just fills.** The executed log is the surviving fleet; the missed signals are the planes that never came back.
**Classify with a single outer merge on (date, ticker, broker)** using `indicator=True`. Three categories fall out of one operation.
**Never let missed/override records mutate the portfolio.** They are pure audit rows, tagged for separate study.
**Preserve intent fields (price, stop, target, risk) on missed trades** — that is the data that reveals *why* you didn't act.
**FIFO with per-lot patching** handles pyramids, partial exits, and reversals in one code path. Pro-rate commission across closed lots; carry the position sign into the P&L calculation.
**Store lots as separate portfolio rows with their own `entry_date`** or FIFO cannot work.
**Make every write idempotent** (check-before-append, patch-same-values). Nightly jobs get re-run.
**Design against friction first.** Pre-populated defaults, dropdowns, phone forms. Automation everywhere data already exists.
**Reward completeness, not performance.** Score the process out of 120; compound a streak multiplier at `1 + streak/20`; forgive one missed weekday.
**Track directional accuracy (`bulls_eye`) *with* the stated reasoning.** Correct calls with bad reasoning are luck; that distinction is the whole point.
**Prompt the AI to analyze behavior, never P&L.** Good psychology can produce a bad week and vice versa.
**Ask whether kaizen entries evolve or merely repeat.** A recurring unchanged intention is a signal to make a structural change, not to try harder.
**Calibrate stops with MAE**, and classify strategies with **MFE/MAE** (>1 trend following, <1 mean reversion).
**Measure drawdowns on all three axes** (depth, duration, frequency) and consecutive losses on two (max run, average run). Size down during losing streaks.
**Watch the pre-vs-post mindset delta.** Sitting at 3 is the goal, not sitting at 5.
